common_name: Louisiana 16 Inch Long Pod Okra (Southern Heirloom with Extra-Long Tender Pods)

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed well beyond last frost; this Louisiana heirloom rewards patience with pods that can stretch far longer than typical okra while staying fry-and-gumbo tender.

directions: Louisiana 16 Inch Long Pod is a tall, vigorous Southern heirloom selected over generations for pods that stay tender even as they grow far beyond the length most okra turns woody. Give plants generous room since they build large leaves and reach considerable height, and consider staking in exposed sites prone to summer storms. Harvest ribbed green pods every day or two once they reach a usable size to keep the heavily branching plant setting new flowers all season. Because it is open-pollinated, seed can be saved from the driest, most mature pods for replanting the following year.

common_name: Stubby Okra (Compact Heirloom with Short Stumpy Pods)

planting.note: Direct sow into warm soil after frost danger has passed; Stubby's shorter stature makes it a good fit for tighter garden rows or raised beds.

directions: Stubby is a shorter heirloom okra, staying noticeably more compact than rangy Southern types while still producing steadily through summer heat. Its blunt, stumpy pods should be picked young, around two to three inches, since the thick shape can turn fibrous quickly once past prime size. The lower profile makes this variety easier to manage in smaller plots or where wind exposure would otherwise call for staking taller okra. Keep pods picked frequently to prevent the compact plant from shutting down seed-pod production early.

common_name: Lee Okra (University of Arkansas Semi-Dwarf Spineless Okra)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed; Lee's compact, mostly unbranched habit suits closer spacing and dense home-garden or trial rows.

directions: Lee was bred at the University of Arkansas from Gulfcoast, Emerald, and Clemson Spineless parentage to give a semi-dwarf plant that stays largely free of side branches, which simplifies picking. Straight, spineless, bright green pods form close along the main stem and should be cut every couple of days at three to four inches for the best texture. The compact, upright habit lets gardeners plant Lee more densely than sprawling heirloom types without sacrificing airflow. Regular harvest keeps the short growing season this variety was bred for producing right up until fall's first cool nights.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture

common_name: Go Big Okra (Burpee Hybrid with Extra-Large Tender Pods)

planting.note: Direct sow once danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Go Big's large mature size calls for wide rows and sturdy support in windy spots.

directions: Go Big is a modern hybrid bred to produce noticeably thick, dark green pods that hold their tenderness at a larger size than most standard okra. Plants grow tall and wide over the season, so give them room to branch and check pods every day or two once production ramps up in midsummer heat. Because the pods stay fry- and stew-worthy even when picked slightly larger, Go Big forgives a missed harvest day better than finer-podded heirlooms. Consistent moisture and full sun keep this vigorous hybrid setting new pods until temperatures cool in fall.

common_name: Millionaire Okra (Early Prolific F1 Hybrid Okra)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed; Millionaire's early maturity makes it a strong choice for gardeners in shorter-summer parts of okra's growing range.

directions: Millionaire is an F1 hybrid bred from Clemson Spineless lines to mature earlier and set pods more heavily than many open-pollinated okra varieties. Sturdy, medium-large plants hold up well to wind and heavy fruit load, producing flavorful pods best cut at three to four inches for peak tenderness. Its early start makes it well suited to regions with a shorter warm season, since it begins yielding before many heirloom types hit their stride. Frequent picking through the heat of summer keeps this vigorous hybrid setting new flowers rather than diverting energy into oversized, fibrous pods.
